root_cause_label: Persistent Regex/Text-Pattern Approach on Binary-Encoded SQLite Data
one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent never parsed the SQLite binary record format; instead it iteratively applied text-based regex patterns to recover stored integer/float values that are binary-encoded, producing incorrect results throughout.
t_err_evidence: At step 9 the agent writes the first recovery script using re.finditer(b'testword\w\w(\d+)', data) — treating stored numeric values as ASCII digit sequences in the binary file, which is wrong because SQLite stores integers and floats in compact binary encoding, not as printable digits.
t_commit_evidence: Once the agent commits to the regex/text-extraction strategy in step 9, all subsequent 92 steps iterate on variations of that same approach (regex patterns, strings utility, struct with guessed offsets) without ever attempting to parse the actual SQLite page/record format, locking in failure from step 9 onward.
t_surface_evidence: At step 14 the output is [{"word": "testword052", "value": 2}] — only one record, with a malformed word key ('testword052' conflates word name and stored value suffix), making it observable that the approach is producing wrong results.
trigger_explanation: The agent lacked knowledge of the SQLite binary file format (page layout, varint/serial-type encoding for stored values). It assumed stored numeric values would appear as ASCII digit sequences adjacent to the text key in the binary file, which is incorrect. The correct approach requires parsing page headers, cell pointers, and SQLite's serial type / varint encoding to decode actual stored integers or IEEE 754 doubles.
forewarning_evidence: Step 7: sqlite3 .dump returns 'ERROR: (26) file is not a database' and ROLLBACK — a clear warning that the database is corrupted/truncated and standard tools will not work, hinting that raw binary parsing is needed. Step 14: the recovered JSON contains only one malformed entry, immediately signaling the text-pattern approach is wrong.
